excerpt_i18n.en: Over the past decade, the market's vision of "AI assistants" has undergone three major rounds of expectation calibration. The first was with the launch of Siri, where voice control brought a novelty in interaction, leading people to believe that the intelligent butler Jarvis from movies was within reach, only to later realize it was often just a voice-activated alarm clock. The second came with the emergence of ChatGPT, whose fluent conversation and reasoning abilities made it seem like AI had finally gained a "brain," but the market soon realized it remained merely a sage confined to dialogue boxes, unable to perceive the world beyond them. In early 2025, the arrival of Manus gave tangible reality to the concept of an Agent. This impact was different from before—many saw for the first time that AI was not only "talking" but also "doing." It opened browsers, wrote code, debugged errors, and even proactively refreshed pages when loading was too slow, all right before your eyes. As the buzz around Manus gradually subsided following its acquisition, people came to realize that, regardless of how the technological shell evolves, humanity's core desire for AI assistants has never changed: users don't just want a chat companion that merely understands speech, nor do they only want a geek tool that writes code in a black-and-white interface; what everyone has always wanted is...

La primera vez fue con el nacimiento de Siri, cuando el control por voz trajo una novedad en la interacción, haciendo creer que el mayordomo inteligente Jarvis de las películas estaba al alcance, pero pronto se descubrió que, en la mayoría de los casos, no era más que un despertador de voz. La segunda vez fue con la aparición de ChatGPT, cuya fluidez en el diálogo y capacidad de razonamiento hicieron pensar que la IA finalmente tenía "cerebro", pero el mercado pronto se dio cuenta de que seguía siendo solo una inteligencia que debatía dentro de un cuadro de diálogo.

Ordering 40 cups of Bawang Tea's 'Bo Ya Jue Xian' in one go. Accessing over 50 government services on Alipay, including visas, household registration, and provident funds. Becoming an AI teaching assistant for every teacher. On January 15, at the Qwen product launch event, Qwen officially announced its full integration into Alibaba's ecosystem, including Taobao, Alipay, Taobao Flash Sales, Fliggy, and Amap, rolling out over 400 new features at once, such as ordering takeout, shopping, and booking flights. AI is transitioning from chatting to getting things done. 

If this Qwen update is merely seen as "adding a few more Alibaba apps," its significance might be underestimated. Wu Jia, President of Alibaba's Qwen C-end Business Group, stated in the opening remarks, "Qwen is the first AI that can truly help you accomplish tasks." The new features span daily life, work, and education, each explained by three product managers on stage. While seemingly scattered, they point to the same shift—Qwen is evolving from a "chat assistant" to a "task assistant." As Wu Jia put it, AI is moving from the passenger seat to the driver's seat.

More importantly, in scenarios like food delivery and e-commerce, Qwen is now touching "transactions" for the first time. Within Alibaba's ecosystem, once a product involves transactions, it is no longer an experimental offering but enters a genuine business validation phase.

This Qwen update may set a new paradigm for the commercial application of AI models. Only after achieving scale has Alibaba begun to "discuss entry points."

Looking back over the past year, the mainstream form of C-end AI applications has largely remained confined to "solving problems within a dialog box."
